# kvrocks

![Version: 0.1.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/Version-0.1.0-informational?style=flat-square) ![Type: application](https://img.shields.io/badge/Type-application-informational?style=flat-square) ![AppVersion: 2.17.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/AppVersion-2.17.0-informational?style=flat-square)

Apache Kvrocks with replication and automatic failover: one master and its replicas, Sentinel for failover, HAProxy as a write endpoint that follows the master.

Sentinel decides who the master is, HAProxy gives clients one address that follows it, and a fencing sidecar stops a master cut off from its peers from taking writes that would be lost. The architecture, what each failure costs and how to operate the chart are in the [repository's README](https://github.com/kinoute/kvrocks-helm).

## Installing

```bash
kubectl create secret generic kvrocks-auth --from-literal=password='change-me'
helm install db oci://ghcr.io/kinoute/charts/kvrocks --version 0.1.0 \
  --set auth.existingSecret=kvrocks-auth
helm test db
```

Until a version is tagged, nothing is published to the registry: replace `oci://ghcr.io/kinoute/charts/kvrocks` with `./helm/kvrocks` from a clone of the repository.

Pick the password before you install: changing it afterwards takes a short write outage, see [Rotating the password](https://github.com/kinoute/kvrocks-helm#rotating-the-password).

With clients over mutual TLS, from certificates you created beforehand:

```yaml
tls:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: db-kvrocks-tls # kubernetes.io/tls, covering db-kvrocks and db-kvrocks-read
  ca:
    secret: db-kvrocks-ca # the CA that signed the client certificates
  clientSecret: db-kvrocks-test-client # a client certificate for `helm test`
```

## Endpoints

For a release named `db`, with the default ports:

| Purpose | Address |
| --- | --- |
| Writes, always the master | `db-kvrocks:6379` |
| Reads, any ready pod (may be slightly stale) | `db-kvrocks-read:6379` |
| Sentinel, for clients that speak it, not with TLS | `db-kvrocks-headless:26379` |

## Requirements

- Kubernetes `>=1.34.0-0`, the oldest version the end-to-end scenarios run on. Sentinel and the fencing loop run as native sidecars.
- Three schedulable nodes with the default `podAntiAffinity: hard`: each Kvrocks pod needs a node of its own.
- Kvrocks 2.16.0 or later in `replication` mode, the first version with `CLIENT PAUSE WRITE`.
- A password without whitespace, double quotes or backslashes: HAProxy sends it in its health checks.

|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| affinity | object | `{}` | Replaces the default affinity entirely. |
| architecture | string | `"replication"` | `replication`: one master and its replicas, with Sentinel failover and an HAProxy write endpoint. `standalone`: a single Kvrocks, no Sentinel, no HAProxy. |
| auth.existingSecret | string | `""` | Name of an existing Secret holding the password. Takes precedence over `password`. |
| auth.password | string | `""` | Password stored in a Secret created by the chart. Prefer `existingSecret`. It must not contain whitespace, double quotes or backslashes. |
| auth.secretKey | string | `"password"` | Key of the password in the Secret. |
| clusterDomain | string | `"cluster.local"` | DNS domain of the cluster, used to build the pods' fully qualified names. |

| config | object | `{"use-rsid-psync":"yes"}` | Extra `kvrocks.conf` settings, as `key: value`. Settings the chart owns (bind, port, dir, the password, the replication role and priority...) are rejected, and so are `rename-command`, which would hide from the chart's scripts the commands they rely on, and the namespace tokens, which are credentials. |
| containerSecurityContext | object | `{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]},"readOnlyRootFilesystem":true}` | Security context of every container of the Kvrocks pods. |
| fencing.enabled | bool | `true` | Pauses the writes of a master that neither a majority of Sentinels nor its replicas follow any more, as when it is cut off from its peers. Kvrocks has no min-replicas-to-write: without fencing, connections already open to such a master keep writing to it until the partition heals, and all those writes are lost. The cost: a healthy master also stops taking writes when it is left without a majority of the pods, two down out of three for instance, as HAProxy already does. |
| fencing.resources | object | `{}` | Resources of the fencing sidecar. |
| fullnameOverride | string | `""` | Overrides the full resource name prefix. The write Service takes exactly this name. |

| global.imageRegistry | string | `""` | Registry that replaces the registry of every image (e.g. a pull-through cache). |
| haproxy.affinity | object | `{}` | Replaces the default affinity, which prefers one HAProxy pod per node. |
| haproxy.check.fall | int | `3` | Failed role checks in a row before HAProxy cuts the connections to a Kvrocks. Higher than 1 so that one slow answer from a busy master does not drop every client. Keep `fall` times `interval` well under `switchover.pauseMilliseconds`: after a handover, the former master holds writes that long, and HAProxy must cut the connections still open to it first. |
| haproxy.check.interval | string | `"1s"` | How often HAProxy asks each Sentinel for the master and each Kvrocks for its role. |

| resources | object | `{}` | Resources of the Kvrocks container. Without any, the pods run as BestEffort and are the first evicted under memory pressure. Kvrocks caches up to 4 GB of blocks by default, on top of its write buffers: with a memory limit, shrink that cache in `config`, or the master is killed for running out of memory, with no handover. The example below is what the scenarios run with on a real cluster. |
